humanities_role_explanation: Humanities topics (including TV shows & movies, art, history, and music) supply more than 50% of the questions in the dataset. However, the benchmark tests general web-browsing agent capabilities (persistent search, multi-hop facts, and constraint satisfaction) rather than domain-specific humanities research methodologies.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: The evaluation dataset consists of text-based questions paired with short-string text reference answers, although the evaluated agents must interact with various text and layout formats on the open web.
analytical_tasks_explanation: The benchmark tasks consist of open-ended QA requiring factual recall of obscure information. Answering correctly requires parsing complex logical and quantitative constraints (e.g., number of TV episodes, soccer match events) and temporal/chronological constraints (e.g., historical date ranges). Models are also evaluated on calibration and uncertainty (confidence estimation) and must execute agentic tool use (persistent web navigation and multi-step search).

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Scoped specifically to evaluating persistent search and information retrieval capabilities of web browsing agents.

evaluates_generative_llm.note: Evaluates OpenAI models including GPT-4o, GPT-4.5, OpenAI o1, and OpenAI Deep Research.

quantitative_metrics.note: Evaluates accuracy (via model-graded semantic equivalence of short-string answers) and calibration error.

published_after_march_2023.note: The paper was published as a preprint in April 2025.

summary: BrowseComp is a challenging benchmark of 1,266 human-curated questions designed to measure an AI agent's ability to persistently browse the web for hard-to-find, multi-constraint information. The benchmark features short, easily verifiable reference answers and acts as a proxy for evaluating search creativity and perseverance under extreme difficulty. Human trainers struggle to solve these tasks, taking hours or giving up entirely in most cases.
key_findings: Standard LLMs perform poorly without specialized search loops, with GPT-4o achieving 0.6% and GPT-4.5 achieving 0.9% accuracy. Enabling web browsing for GPT-4o only yields 1.9% accuracy, while the reasoning model OpenAI o1 reaches 9.9%. OpenAI Deep Research, designed for persistent browsing, achieves 51.5% accuracy, which scales smoothly with increased test-time compute. Employing confidence-based Best-of-N voting further improves Deep Research performance by up to 25%.
facets_explanation: The reference answers were created by contracted human trainers who formulated questions based on personal interests with single, short, and indisputable answers. Answering these questions requires extensive open-web browsing because the stimulus itself contains only complex search constraints, making the task heavily reliant on knowledge beyond the stimulus. Any ambiguity, multiple possible answers, or errors discovered during human cross-verification or model testing led to question revision or deletion, showing that plurality was treated as noise.
results_explanation: The paper reports a headline accuracy of 51.5% for the best-performing model, 'Deep Research' (Table 3). Humans solved 29.2% of the tasks ('Solved by human 367 / 1,255 (29.2%)', Table 2), resulting in a human gap of -22.3 percentage points (rounded to -22). No performance gaps between task formats or difficulty splits are reported for the same model, and cultural asymmetry is not stated.
